html:
I spent four years doing a PhD in Germany.

When I arrived I knew only basics like Danke and Bitte, plus a little grammar. My officemate (an Israeli) was fanatical about languages, and I’m very interested in languages myself, so from my first days at the institute I seized every chance to speak German. At first it was a disaster, naturally, and I often left Germans with no idea what I meant. With the shameless attitude that “if my German is bad, they’re the ones who suffer,” within about six months of arriving I had given up English entirely in everyday conversation (except on academic topics).

My grammar still isn’t solid and I make all kinds of mistakes when I speak, but as long as you dare to speak, Germans will basically get your point. After two years I could discuss research in German and started trying to teach lab classes in German. I’ve now been away from Germany for over a year, and my German has slipped quite a bit. Looking back, by the time I left, my German was somewhere between B1 and B2. I learned German the wild way, quite differently from how I learned English as a child. Ranking the four skills from strongest to weakest, mine go: speaking > reading > listening > writing. Reading moved up a place in my last year because I took my German driving test in German. I don’t need to write research papers in German, so I don’t much mind that writing is my weakest. For more formal emails you can look up templates, and for ordinary emails there’s no real problem as long as the meaning is clear.

I also took quite a few German classes, always with speaking as my goal (if you need to pass an exam, this advice isn’t for you). I tried the university, the Volkshochschule (a community adult-education center) and Inlingua. The first two lean toward exam-style grammar, reading and writing. Inlingua helped me most: once the essential grammar is covered, it’s mostly about speaking, and classes are small (about ten people), so you get lots of attention and plenty of chances to talk. Still, if you really want to raise your spoken German, making German friends and chatting with Germans is by far the most efficient way. Most universities run language-partner programs, and there are similar groups on Facebook. In a bachelor’s program, your class is bound to have far more local students than foreigners, so join in and chat with them whenever you can (though German circles aren’t especially easy to break into), and speak German with your international classmates as much as possible too.

You’re only in your first year and so young, so you’re bound to pick it up much faster. Good luck.

That’s all.

Curious about the years a guy from Northeast China has spent knocking around European academia and industry? See my Zhihu column PhD Diaries.
